name: Fernando Mendoza
blurb: Mendoza’s storybook college career is one of the most compelling parts of the No. 1 overall pick. From his humble beginnings as a lightly recruited three-star QB to transferring to Indiana and having a season for the ages, which ended in an undefeated national championship. He jumped in every single meaningful statistical category and became Indiana’s first-ever Heisman Trophy winner and the first in the Big Ten since 2006. The Raiders are starting fresh with play-caller Klint Kubiak at the helm. In Year 1, Mendoza will likely take some lumps. He is off the redraft radar, waiting his turn to start behind veteran Kirk Cousins.

name: Jeremiyah Love
blurb: The Notre Dame superstar became the highest draft RB since Saquon Barkley after the Cardinals selected him third overall. His combination of size, speed, early breakout age (19.3), and production is a recipe for success at the next level. Tyler Allgeier could steal some goal-line looks and temper expectations for fantasy. His weekly workload will be in question despite the fact that RBs drafted inside the top 10 have averaged 19+ touches per game in Year 1 over the last decade. We have Love ranked as an RB2 for 2026, but his Week 1 outlook is now in question. He exited Arizona's first preseason game with a high ankle sprain and is expected to miss the remainder of the preseason.

name: Carnell Tate
blurb: Tennessee surprised a lot of folks in April when they took Carnell Tate fourth overall in the NFL Draft. That type of draft capital suggests he will be on the field right away as an every-down player with the chance to lead the team in production. It can take time for rookie WRs to develop throughout the year, so even if Tate doesn’t get off to a fast start, he is a player who could really provide a boost to your squad late in the year.

name: Jordyn Tyson
blurb: With Kellen Moore’s offense projecting to be among the league leaders in pace and play volume and the Saints not really having a reliable third option in the receiver room, we think both Olave and Tyson can eat this year. Of course, we are projecting Olave as the #1 option, especially after Tyson suffered yet another hamstring injury in training camp. He's expected to miss about two months, which means he's going to miss multiple regular season games. He's beginning the season on IR, which makes him a tough click in redraft leagues given the injury risk unless your league uses an IR spot. That said, if he can get healthy, the late-season upside is real if the Saints offense takes a leap in Year 2 of the Kellen Moore era.

name: Ty Simpson
blurb: After starting just 15 total games at Alabama, the Rams made one of the most shocking picks of the draft, taking Simpson 13th overall. Beyond the optics of drafting a first-round QB to back up the league MVP (ask Green Bay), we know Simpson will likely take a year or two to learn behind Matthew Stafford. The lack of starting experience is a red flag in his profile and a common thread among failed highly drafted QBs who busted in the NFL. Regardless, it is tough to doubt what McVay and his crew do as they continually compete in the NFC.

name: Kenyon Sadiq
blurb: Sadiq’s impressive athletic profile (remember when he broke almost every record at the NFL Combine?) catapulted him into the first round, heading to the New York Jets at pick 16. The question marks related to his usage at Oregon remain, as fantasy managers must question if a man who couldn’t top 600 receiving yards during his final year in college will be successful as a Jet with Geno Smith under center? He could end up second or third on the team in targets behind WR Garrett Wilson and RB Breece Hall, while competing with fellow rookie Omar Cooper Jr. Oh, and there is also a feline in Mason Taylor in the room that Sadiq has to overtake on the depth chart. Between you and me, a dawg always wins over a cat. You probably aren’t counting on Sadiq right away in redraft this year, but his time will eventually come.

name: Makai Lemon
blurb: After the A.J. Brown trade to New England, rookie Makai Lemon should step into a starting role right away as a rookie across from DeVonta Smith. The 2025 Biletnikoff Award winner in college, Lemon’s production during his final season at USC was excellent, but the one question mark entering the NFL is whether or not he can play on the perimeter, as he was primarily a slot player in college. Philly’s offense should look a lot different this year with a new OC in town. If he is as talented as the production profile suggests and Jalen Hurts can bounce back as a passer, Lemon has a chance to be a meaningful difference maker for fantasy in 2026 and enter WR3 territory. That said, Lemon might get off to a slower start as he's missed valuable time in both mini camp and training camp because of a hamstring injury.

name: KC Concepcion
blurb: The Browns took KC with the 24th overall pick in April’s draft as the first skill position pick in the Todd Monken era. Clearly, they have a plan for the young WR, but this could be a frustrating situation to start the year. Jerry Jeudy and Cedric Tillman could still see some snaps, and the QB room is gross. We like him as a potential breakout candidate in the back half of the season when rookies tend to emerge, and with his ADP likely to remain suppressed due to the stink of the Browns, you can take him late in drafts and stash him to see what shakes out in Cleveland.

name: Omar Cooper Jr.
blurb: How many fantasy options can this version of Geno Smith support in 2026? We know Garrett Wilson and Breece Hall are likely to dominate touches here, so any secondary Jets players are probably going to have to get there via efficiency. Call us crazy, but if your eyeballs saw Geno playing QB last season, we are a little hesitant with that bet! That is where the concern comes in for a guy like Cooper, who profiles as a possession and yards after the catch WR in the NFL. So long as Garrett Wilson is healthy, Cooper’s fantasy upside will be capped, but you could always target him late in drafts and see what shakes out in New York early in the season. Rookie WRs are generally good bets at ADP because the cost is reasonable, but if we are comparing Cooper to the other first-round NFL draft picks, he is not as big of a priority as guys like Carnell Tate, Makai Lemon, or Jordyn Tyson.

name: Jadarian Price
blurb: After much speculation before the NFL Draft, the Seahawks took the Notre Dame RB with the final pick of Round 1. Price’s selection looks even stronger, knowing we did not see another RB drafted until the end of Round 3. His initial burst plus his contact balance make for a lethal combo, although he was not utilized much in the passing game in college, with just 15 total receptions over three years. With Zach Charbonnet on the mend from an ACL injury, Price found arguably the best landing spot for a rookie RB in 2026. The Seahawks are favored in each of their first 10 matchups. We have him ranked as a high-end FLEX/RB2 option with the expectation that his draft stock could rise as get closer to Week 1.

name: De'Zhaun Stribling
blurb: The Niners shocked everyone by taking De’Zhaun Stribling 33rd overall in the NFL Draft. He was projected by most as a Day 2 guy, but no one saw this coming. It suggests they have a plan for him, and with Ricky Pearsall battling knee issues at the start of camp, he could be more than just a role player in Year 1. San Francisco did bring back Deebo on a one-year deal after Pearsall's latest knee injury, so perhaps it pours some cold water on the Stribling hype. Still, he profiles as a guy who could play on the perimeter across from Evans, and the camp reviews have been excellent. You can throw a dart late in your draft and stash him with minimal risk. We're in!

name: Denzel Boston
blurb: Entering the 2026 season, it is possible Boston is playing behind Jerry Jeudy and KC Concepcion to start the season. For now, we view him as a name to monitor throughout the early part of the year rather than a priority redraft target. Perhaps he can come on late in the year to provide some late-season rookie upside.

name: Germie Bernard
blurb: Germie probably needs an injury to one of DK Metcalf or Michael Pittman to be fantasy relevant this year. We are projecting him to play in the slot for Pittsburgh, and while that role could provide plenty of value for the Steelers, we are skeptical that it turns into enough fantasy points to make him a startable asset. The rookie is worth monitoring throughout camp, but for now, he is nothing more than a late-round stash.

name: Eli Stowers
blurb: The consensus TE2 behind Sadiq heading into the NFL Draft is now connected to one of the NFC perennial powers. After a final year at Vandy, where he won the 2025 John Mackey award as college football’s top TE, Stowers' production profile was quite strong, leading the class in targets per route run. Stowers will be listed as a TE, but he is essentially a big hybrid WR/TE who actually began college as a QB. He will be behind Dallas Goedert on the depth chart, making him hard to roster in redraft in 2026 outside of an injury.

name: Nate Boerkircher
blurb: Boerkircher (pronounced BOAR-kur-chur) was a surprise second-round selection by the Jaguars. The draft capital is enough to make you pay attention, but when you look back at his performance in college, you are left wanting more - he never topped more than 22 targets in college. Just called him “Boerkircher the Blocker” as that will probably be his main task in Jacksonville.

name: Marlin Klein
blurb: The Texans really reached on Klein, grabbing the Michigan TE in the second round when most had a Day 3 grade on him. Texans, what do you know that we don’t?! Klein’s college production was lacking, but he did play behind one Mr. LOVEland, so maybe that is somewhat excusable… For redraft purposes, ignore and move on.

name: Max Klare
blurb: Before transferring to Ohio State for his final year, Klare was a production monster at Purdue and showcased target-earning ability that could intrigue at the next level. Unfortunately, his first-year prospects are dim as he was selected by the Rams, who collect TEs like it is going out of style. Los Angeles has Colby Parkinson, Tyler Higbee, Terrance Ferguson, and Davis Allen on the roster, making the rookie just another guy in the room. Sean McVay has shown a strong proclivity to running 13-personnel, so we know Klare will be rotated in.

name: Carson Beck
blurb: The Cardinals selected Beck in the third round, making him the third QB taken in the draft. His experience (43 college starts) certainly helped his cause after the team brought him in for a top-30 visit. He can get the ball out quickly on 3-step drops and hit his receivers in stride in zone coverage. His arm strength is subpar, but it should not shock anyone if Beck ends up finishing the season as the Cardinals' starting QB on a team destined for a top-5 pick.

name: Sam Roush
blurb: The Stanford man with the taped-together glasses heads to Chicago as the sixth TE off the board. We enjoy the draft capital, we love that he had the fourth-highest amount of targets in this class, and we love his solid 6.5 YAC/REC. What do we not love? The level of depth in this depth chart. Since everywhere you turn in the windy city, there is an offensive weapon, Roush will probably be spending most of his time blocking.

name: Antonio Williams
blurb: Terry McLaurin figures to be option A, B, and C in Washington. Behind him, this depth chart is yucky. Deebo Samuel is gone, and the Commanders did very little to replace him in free agency. Enter Williams, who has a chance to be the #2 option right away as a rookie. One question mark on Williams is how his game will translate to the NFL after he ran almost 80% of his routes from the slot in college. We expect him to start out as the team’s primary slot WR, and hopefully, he can jump into 2WR sets. If not, his ceiling is probably capped for fantasy. Even so, his ADP is so late that we don’t mind taking a shot on him in drafts and stashing him to see how things play out early in the season.

name: Oscar Delp
blurb: There was a lot of chatter around what could have been with Oscar Delp, but looking at his numbers from college, he never really delivered. He never hit 300 receiving yards at Georgia thanks to competition with some guy named Brock Bowers basically running the offense during Delp’s first two seasons. Even with questions on the production profile, the Saints grabbed him in the third round to add youth to their TE room. He will have a tough time making an impact in redraft this year, presumably buried on the TE depth chart behind Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant.

name: Malachi Fields
blurb: The Giants traded multiple picks to land Notre Dame’s Malachi Fields, so the new staff likely has a role in mind for him. At 6’5” and 218 pounds, he is a true X receiver. Unfortunately, for fantasy, Fields looks like a guy who is more likely to help the Giants than help our fantasy teams, as he is a pretty weak prospect coming out of Notre Dame. We know Malik Nabers is the alpha when healthy, and the team paid big money to Isaiah Likely in free agency. We would be surprised if he is able to generate enough volume to matter for fantasy, but he could have some TD upside in the right matchups thanks to his power forward frame.

name: Caleb Douglas
blurb: The Dolphins entered the NFL Draft with easily the weakest WR depth chart in the league. No offense, Caleb, but this selection in the NFL Draft did very little to change that. Douglas was overdrafted based on consensus big boards and, analytically, was a pretty weak prospect. Still, if you are in a deeper league, you should at least know the name, as the opportunity to see the field as a rookie is there. If you want to have a little giggle, just go look at the Dolphins’ depth chart.

name: Drew Allar
blurb: Going into the 2025 season, Allar was projected by many to be a top-10 pick in the NFL Draft. He suffered a pretty big fall from grace in a lost season at Penn State with alot of missed opportunities as the team asked him to do more, especially against man coverage. The upside is there, but will Pittsburgh give him the opportunity behind Aaron Rodgers?

name: Zachariah Branch
blurb: We know Drake London is the dude here in Atlanta, but behind him, this depth chart is wide open. The Falcons used the 79th overall pick on the former Georgia Bulldog, so he has a realistic opportunity to see the field as a rookie. Electric in the return game and dangerous with the ball in his hands, Branch was used primarily in the screen game and on manufactured touches in college. He is going to have to develop in the NFL to be a factor for fantasy, but perhaps he can be a late-season riser.

name: Ja'Kobi Lane
blurb: Lane saw a bunch of contested catches at USC, which is interesting considering his slender build. Expect him to start the season behind Flowers and Rashod Bateman in a part-time role with the chance to develop over the course of his rookie season. For now, he is not worth looking at in fantasy drafts.

name: Chris Brazzell II
blurb: At 6’4” and 198 pounds, Brazzell has the prototypical perimeter deep threat build. He will likely compete with Xavier Legette for playing time as a rookie and be a part-time contributor, especially late in the year. We're not expecting the rookie to do much early on given that he suffered a knee injury in training camp that could sideline him for all of August. After all, are we really that excited about the third or fourth option in a Bryce Young offense? No offense, Bryce!

name: Ted Hurst III
blurb: Tampa took Hurst in the third round of the NFL Draft as he was one of the biggest risers throughout the pre-draft process. Keep expectations in check for Year 1, however. Even though Mike Evans is gone, Egbuka and Godwin are still here, and Jalen McMillan has been productive whenever he has been healthy. Throw in the fact that the Bucs brought in one of the league’s top pass-catching backs in Kenny Gainwell, and it is really tough to see many targets in Year 1 for Hurst. Know the name just in case someone in the Bucs’ WR room gets banged up this year.

name: Will Kacmarek
blurb: The Dolphins desperately needed pass catchers as they entered the draft, so why not draft a converted DE-to-TE in the third round? Duh! All joking aside, Kacmarek will be the blocking TE for Miami spending more time looking out for Malik Willis than looking out for balls from Malik Willis. With only 15 receptions during his final year at Ohio State, you can cross him off your redraft considerations.

name: Zavion Thomas
blurb: With Mr. LOVEland, Luther Burden, and Rome Odunze atop the pecking order, Thomas isn’t on the radar for redraft leagues. Expect him to be a part-time player and contribute on special teams. He did log 40 carries in college and had 95 combined kickoff and punt returns, so he brings some versatility to Chicago, but this is not a guy you need to worry about in your redraft league.

name: Kaelon Black
blurb: Despite a lackluster production profile, Black was a hot commodity in pre-draft visits, meeting with 10 teams before the 49ers surprisingly selected him 90th overall. Kyle Shanahan offenses always surprise us with the names that leap from obscurity, but this one was a head scratcher. CMC is coming off a season where he touched the ball 413 times, so perhaps we see Black worked into the mix. Pay attention to camp reports to see where he lands on the depth chart, competing with Jordan James and Isaac Guerendo for backup duties.

name: Chris Bell
blurb: Bell was viewed in league circles as a fringe first-round NFL Draft pick before tearing his ACL in 2025. Because of the injury, he fell to the third round and landed in an intriguing spot. Unfortunately, because of the ACL recovery, we are not expecting Bell to be 100% in training camp, which, for a rookie, is not ideal when you are trying to learn the ropes of the NFL. Look for him to be more of a factor late in the season and in 2027.

name: Eli Raridon
blurb: The Patriots took their first offensive skill player in the third round with Raridon, who had a solid final year at Notre Dame highlighted by his 2.23 yards per route run. He looks like the next man up behind Hunter Henry on a good team with a talented QB. With a solid athletic profile, he is one of the few “non-blocking” Day 2 TEs from this year’s draft to know for the future.

name: Brenen Thompson
blurb: This is the exact type of player Mike McDaniel lies awake at night thinking about how to get the ball in his hands to flip the field. He has elite, home-run-hitting speed, but we would be really surprised if he is a high-volume player at the next level. Ladd is the top guy here, while Oronde Gadsden and Quentin Johnston should see plenty of looks. Meanwhile, the team is reportedly high on last year’s second-round pick, Tre’ Harris. Expect Thompson to have a few spike weeks, but good luck predicting them.

name: Jonah Coleman
blurb: With an early breakout age (20) and 25 rushing TDs over his final two seasons, he was the engine of the Huskies offense post-Michael Penix Jr. years. Coleman’s draft stock slipped after a lack of testing, but the landing spot in Denver should put him on your radar. Sean Payton loves utilizing an RB committee more than his own family, as Coleman begins the season third or fourth on the RB depth chart. Keep your head on a swivel, knowing Coleman could have a moment as a priority waiver pickup.

name: Cade Klubnik
blurb: Klubnik is another QB in this class that massively lost out on millions of NFL dollars following a down 2025 season. His junior season was by far his best campaign, highlighted by 3,600+ passing yards with an impressive 36:6 TD:INT ratio. After garnering off-season Heisman hype, the Clemson Tigers nosedived to a 7-5 record, and Klubnik went from a potential first-round pick to a Day 3 selection by the Jets. We will see how many starts Geno Smith receives before giving way to Klubnik as New York likely looks to 2027 for their QB answers.

name: Elijah Sarratt
blurb: There are talks of Sarratt moving into the ‘Big Slot’ role in Year 1 in Baltimore, which is kind of intriguing in deep formats. Sarratt is a ball winner who was frequently used in the red zone in college, giving him life as a contributor right away as a rookie in Baltimore. That said, we expect Flowers and Bateman to open the season as the top WRs on the depth chart, and the Ravens have never had a high pass rate in the Lamar Jackson era, so the path for fantasy is pretty thin out of the gate. He is not on the radar right now as a redraft target, but know the name for the waiver wire in the event Flowers or Bateman miss time due to injury.

name: Kaden Wetjen
blurb: Wetjen?! What a cool name. That is about where the positives end for fantasy. DK Metcalf, Michael Pittman, and Germie Bernard are the top options here. No, thank you!

name: Mike Washington Jr.
blurb: If you are looking for a “big-bodied back” from this class, Big Mike might be your style. He blew the doors off the combine but landed on a Vegas team that has franchise RB Ashton Jeanty blocking his path to fantasy relevance. New HC Klint Kubiak did utilize a two-back system in Seattle, so perhaps Washington works his way into the rotation more than we realize, especially after showing out in the preseason. We view him as one of the higher priority insurance RBs, especially after Ashton Jeanty picked up an ankle injury in late August.

name: Skyler Bell
blurb: The Bills sure do have a type, don’t they? Khalil Shakir and DJ Moore do their best work in the short-to-intermediate area, where they can win after the catch. That is kind of what Bell does best, too, so he is a fit in Joe Brady’s offense. Unfortunately, given that Moore, Shakir, and Josh Palmer are atop the depth chart, we are not sure he will carve out a consistent role as a rookie.

name: Matt Hibner
blurb: With the departure of Isaiah Likely, some were wondering if the Ravens were going to add to the TE room. We got our answer when Matthew Hibner was the first TE taken in the fourth round. The man loves college, spending four years at Michigan and two at SMU, yet never topped 1.37 yards per route run. He is behind Mark Andrews and Durham Smythe on the depth chart and shouldn’t be relevant in redraft this year, even with his higher-end athleticism.

name: Bryce Lance
blurb: Does this name sound familiar? It should! Bryce is the younger brother of superstar NFL QB Trey Lance (We’ll never quit you, Trey!). He gets a boost in the ranks just for that, obviously. In all seriousness, he is a fun player who can help the Saints in a unique role. Running in the 4.3s at the Combine, Lance provides a home run threat in Kellen Moore’s offense. In theory, that sounds good, but when Chris Olave and Jordyn Tyson are on the team, there is unlikely to be enough volume for it to matter for fantasy.

name: Colbie Young
blurb: With Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins dominating volume here, Young is going to be a part-time role player in 2026. Even if one of those guys missed time with an injury, we are not even sure Young has the talent to capitalize. No need worry about this fella in your redraft league.

name: Reggie Virgil
blurb: Reggie Virgil is a fifth-round pick out of Texas Tech who is now competing with Trey McBride, Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson, and Jeremiyah Love for targets. So, you guys won’t believe this, but we are not looking Virgil’s way for fantasy. Sorry, Reggie. It’s not personal.

name: Justin Joly
blurb: “JOE-lee, JOE-lee, JOE-lee, JOE-leeeeee”. All the Dolly Parton fans out there are rejoicing in the correct pronunciation of this fifth-round TE. The converted WR has lower draft capital than we would like, but the team did trade up to take him. Joly had the second-most TDs in his draft class, and his skill with contested catches could make him a solid red zone option for Bo Nix. Do not expect production significant enough to make him relevant in redraft for 2026.

name: Max Bredeson
blurb: Bredeson was drafted in the fifth round to be an FB/TE as the replacement for retired Viking CJ Ham. Even with his experience all over the field, he will likely see the field for blocking and special teams dirty work. This is great for the Vikings, not for our fantasy rosters.

name: Emmett Johnson
blurb: Johnson slowly made it into the good graces of Nebraska HC Matt "Ha" Rhule, morphing into one of college football's premier workhorses in 2025. His rough combine metrics hurt his stock as he fell all the way to KC in the fifth round, way behind his projected draft position among consensus boards. He is the classic production-versus-combine metrics discussion at the RB position and now finds himself firmly behind Kenneth Walker III with the Chiefs cutting ties with Emari Demercado.

name: Tanner Koziol
blurb: The Jags double-dipped in the TE well, blocking Nate Boerkircher in the second round and following up with Koziol with pick 164. Koziol is big - 6’7” big - and led Houston in receptions his final year. The draft capital will put him behind Boerkircher in the rotation as he likely will be a special teamer in Year 1.

name: Nicholas Singleton
blurb: The former #1 RB recruit in the nation finished his four-year career at Penn State as Penn State's all-time rushing TD leader with 45! Unfortunately, after suffering a foot injury during a Senior Bowl practice, Singleton's draft stock fell to the fifth round. If you believe in his size/speed combo, perhaps he can eventually overtake Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears and turn into a team's lead back in the back half of the season.

name: Kendrick Law
blurb: Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell love to draft some dawgs with some grit. Hey, Law at least has that going for him. He is built like a RB and forced plenty of missed tackles in college. Unfortunately, the rookie tore his ACL in early June and will miss all of 2026.

name: Riley Nowakowski
blurb: Riley was a big fan of the collegiate experience spending five years at Wisconsin before finishing with a National Championship at Indiana. He has played all over the field (linebacker, a fullback, and on special teams) before ultimately being drafted as a TE. He is now on the Steelers roster as a fullback. Let’s call a spade a spade: he ain’t making it onto any redraft rosters in 2026.

name: Joe Royer
blurb: The Browns really nailed this draft. Offense-wise, after double-dipping on WRs with KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston, they came back in Round 5 to grab Cincinnati’s Joe Royer, keeping the Ohio boy in the state. The team has Harold Fannin Jr. atop the depth chart, but past that, the runway is open for Royer. The Browns led the league in 12 personnel in 2025, now if they could just find their franchise QB…

name: Josh Cuevas
blurb: Baltimore loves to pair a blocking and receiving TE in a draft. They did it again in 2026 taking Cuevas on Day 3, 40 picks after Matthew Hibner. Cuevas is less athletic than Hibner, and even though he has experience with a couple of different NFL-style offenses with time spent at Cal Poly, Washington, and Alabama, he will probably be used sparingly in the passing game, at least in 2026.

name: Adam Randall
blurb: Randall came to Clemson as a highly regarded WR and ended his senior year as an intriguing RB prospect after collecting 13 total TDs and 36 receptions. He was taken on Day 3, most notably as someone hand-selected by the team’s owner, which is either the best thing or the worst thing, depending on your point of view. Perhaps he can earn the RB2 role behind the Big Dog, but the most likely outcome is that he is just a role player in Year 1. Randall is beginning the season on IR because of injury.

name: Cyrus Allen
blurb: Allen led the Cincinnati Bearcats in targets, catches, and receiving yards in 2025, and his 13 receiving TDs were tied for the third-most in the FBS. He had solid production throughout his collegiate career, but obviously, he fell to Day 3 for a reason. We are always interested in Mahomes' pass catchers, but for now, he is more of a name to monitor in camp than a guy you need to pick in your redraft league.

name: Kevin Coleman Jr.
blurb: The Dophins took a quantity over quality approach at the WR position in the 2026 NFL Draft. They double-dipped on Day 2, then took Coleman in the fifth round. He was in the slot on over 90% of his career college snaps, so it is pretty clear he will be pigeon-holed into that role in the NFL. Malik Washington, who comes from the previous regime, is projected as the top slot guy right now, so it’s not hard to envision a scenario where he is getting some snaps as the year progresses. Maybe he will be a deep waiver wide add late in the season when it’s #NastyBoy Szn.

name: Cole Payton
blurb: The NDSU product won some scouts over at the Combine with an awesome display of athleticism as one of the bigger lefty prospects (6'3", 232 lbs.) in recent memory. His 40" vertical and 10'10" broad jump were both 80th percentile marks for QBs, and his 31 career rushing TDs are noteworthy. However, with Tanner McKee and Andy Dalton starting ahead of him on the Philly depth chart behind Jalen Hurts, you likely will not see him much this year. He projects as a niche backup with perhaps some packages ala Taysom Hill near the goal line as a runner.

name: Seydou Traore
blurb: An ex-soccer player born in France (bonjour!), Traore spent the majority of his youth playing goal-keeper. An intriguing athletic profile, Traore needs more time to cultivate the nuances of the TE position, but he lands on a team in Miami that needs pass-catchers so badly, it may be trial by fire for him. Greg Dulcich sits atop the depth chart, and fellow rookie Will Kacmarek just below. He is a fun story but not one we are paying attention to for redraft purposes.

name: Taylen Green
blurb: Another QB for Cleveland?! The 6’6” Green came into college with a track and field background, morphing into a true unicorn when it comes to the type of QB traits we drool over for fantasy. After redshirting and two seasons as the starter at Boise State, Green entered the transfer portal, landing in the SEC, and started 24 games the past two seasons at Arkansas. He is raw and likely will ride the bench all season, but you can squint and see the tools that might make him attractive as a developmental prospect at the next level.

name: Bauer Sharp
blurb: An ex-QB with one of the best names out there, Sharp has very little to turn heads profile-wise. He jumped around schools and finished at LSU, where he finished with a dodgy stat line of 248 yards receiving on 31 targets. He may stand a better chance as a secret agent with that name than getting on an NFL field as a starting TE. Apologies Bauer.

name: Kaytron Allen
blurb: Nicknamed "the Fatman" by his mother, Allen came into Penn State as a highly regarded recruit and got to work in the gym. He checks a lot of the physical profile boxes we want at the next level, and finished his college career as Penn State's all-time leader in rush attempts and rushing yards. The question is whether his lack of flash and creativity as a runner will cap him at the next level. He likely begins third or fourth on the Washington depth chart.

name: Barion Brown
blurb: Brown finished his career at LSU, but before that, he was at Kentucky, where he set the school record for career kickoff return average. Unfortunately, we don’t get fantasy points for that, but it is a sneaky add for the Saints in the special teams department and the manufactured touches department.

name: Josh Cameron
blurb: With Brian Thomas Jr., Jakobi Meyers, and Parker Washington (and maybe even Travis Hunter) entrenched as starters, Cameron will be fighting for scraps. No need to worry about this fella in your redraft league.

name: Malik Benson
blurb: You can squint and see it. To be fair, you have to squint really hard. But if you just keep squinting, you can see a world where Benson sees the field. No disrespect to future Hall of Famers Jalen Nailor, Jack Bech, and Tre Tucker, but this WR room is pretty weak. It wouldn’t be shocking to see the Raiders want to get a look at their rookie late in the season. For now, he is just a guy worth monitoring throughout training camp.

name: CJ Daniels
blurb: The only reason Daniels would be on the radar for fantasy is if Puka Nacua and/or Davante Adams got injured. To be fair, that could happen, but even so, Daniels is a shaky prospect at best who will need to earn the trust of Stafford and Sean McVay.

name: Demond Claiborne
blurb: Claiborne slipped to the sixth round, albeit in a solid landing spot for the future, as both Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason are in the final year of their deals. His experience as a kick returner shows on the field, but dear Lord, Claiborne needs to take care of the football. He frequently was stuffed at the line of scrimmage, fumbled the football, or had concentration issues in the passing game.

name: Emmanuel Henderson Jr.
blurb: Henderson is a deep threat who also contributed in the return game while in college, so he projects as a low-volume role player in the NFL. With JSN, Cooper Kupp, and Rashid Shaheed atop the depth chart, Henderson Jr. is probably going to be a special teams contributor in Year 1.

name: CJ Williams
blurb: The Jags’ WR room is loaded right now. They’ve got BTJ, Parker Washington, and Jakobi Meyers locked in, and that doesn’t even include whatever WR snaps we get from Travis Hunter this season. Sorry, CJ. It ain’t gonna happen, buddy.

name: Lewis Bond
blurb: Bond…Lewis Bond. We call him .007 because that’s exactly how many fantasy points he will score this year. In all seriousness, Big Lew is buried on the depth chart for a run-heavy team. No thank ya!

name: Anthony Smith
blurb: Any fantasy value for an ancillary WR on the Cowboys completely went out the window when George Pickens signed his franchise tag. With CeeDee and Pickens dominating targets, there won't be much to go around for the depth guys, especially someone like Smith, who wasn’t drafted until the seventh round.

name: Jack Endries
blurb: A walk-on at Cal, Endries led the team in receiving in 2024 with future Heisman-winning Fernando Mendoza at the helm. His journey to relevance in the NFL will not be that easy. He lands on a team with a strong QB at the helm but is surrounded by pass-catchers who will always get the look before him. Even with decent athleticism and college production, you won’t be glancing Endries’ way this season.

name: Athan Kaliakmanis
blurb: Now that is a fun name. The Rutgers QB completed just 56% of his passes in college, and it will be a miracle if he sees the field in 2026 behind Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota.

name: Jaren Kanak
blurb: Another Day 3 TE, another guy at the bottom of the depth chart. Kanak is a real Swiss army knife when it comes to positions - he has experience playing linebacker, QB, and WR! Kanak was born for special teams, not for being rostered in fantasy.

name: Eli Heidenreich
blurb: Heidenreich’s 2025 season feels like someone took over with the XBOX controller and decided to go ham. Operating in Navy’s “Wing-T” offense as a hybrid RB/WR/FB, he dominated as a receiver with 941 receiving yards. He should see work on special teams and perhaps eventually mix in as a third-down back. As fun a player as he is, let us remember this is a seventh-round pick buried on the depth chart.

name: Behren Morton
blurb: Morton guided Texas Tech to a perfect 11-0 record before missing the rest of his senior year with a knee injury. He joins Tommy DeVito as a backup behind star QB Drake Maye.

name: Seth McGowan
blurb: McGowan has been around the block, starting out at Oklahoma way back in 2020, being in jail for three months, and out of football for two years, playing at Butler junior college in 2023, New Mexico State in 2024, and finally, Kentucky in 2025. Whew. Did you get all that? He will fight for special teams snaps in 2026.

name: Jam Miller
blurb: “You just got jammed!” As fun a phrase that might be holding in your back pocket for the right moment, Miller barely went drafted in April. Ask Alabama fans where it went wrong, as he entered college as a record-setting high school RB recruit, who steadily decreased in efficiency and production throughout his college career. Expect Miller not to see much of the field in 2026.

name: Carsen Ryan
blurb: Going off the board near the very end of the draft to the Cleveland Browns is rarely a good thing for anyone, Carsen Ryan included. He is buried on a depth chart led by Harold Fannin Jr., and even with the departure of David Njoku, there are pass-catchers ahead that will step up way before Ryan. No need to remember he exists in our NFL universe.

name: Garrett Nussmeier
blurb: Woof. What a fall for the LSU QB. Before the 2025 season, he was seen as a top-10 NFL Draft pick. Injuries and inconsistency killed his draft stock. His 9 & 1/8th inch hands were a 13th percentile mark, and he did not participate in any speed or jumping-related drills at the Combine. Backing up Mahomes is not the worst gig in the world!

name: Deion Burks
blurb: Michael Pittman’s departure theoretically opens up the door for a sleeper to emerge, but we have major question marks on Burks’ ability to play in the NFL. He crushed at the Combine, running in the 4.3s, but that is about where the positives end from an analytical perspective.

name: Dallen Bentley
blurb: A solid blocking TE, Bentley is relatively new to the position and lands in Denver, where he is at the bottom of an extremely deep TE depth chart. I mean, who can dare top Adam Trautman, amirite? No, really, Bentley is going to be developmental at best, off the roster at worst,  and potentially out of the league before you finish reading this sentence.
